stage_directions: Enter LEONATO, HERO, BEATRICE and others, with a Messenger.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: I learn in this letter that Don Pedro of Arragon comes this night

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: to Messina.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: He is very near by this: he was not three leagues off when I left

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: him.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: How many gentlemen have you lost in this action?

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: But few of any sort, and none of name.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: A victory is twice itself when the achiever brings home full numbers.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: I find here that Don Pedro hath bestowed much honour on a young

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: Florentine called Claudio.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: Much deserved on his part, and equally remembered by Don Pedro.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: He hath borne himself beyond the promise of his age, doing in the

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: figure of a lamb the feats of a lion: he hath indeed better bettered

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: expectation than you must expect of me to tell you how.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: He hath an uncle here in Messina will be very much glad of it.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: I have already delivered him letters, and there appears much joy in

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: him; even so much that joy could not show itself modest enough without

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: a badge of bitterness.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: Did he break out into tears?

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: In great measure.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: A kind overflow of kindness. There are no faces truer than those that

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: are so washed; how much better is it to weep at joy than to joy at

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: weeping!

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: I pray you, is Signior Mountanto returned from the wars or no?

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: I know none of that name, lady: there was none such in the army

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: of any sort.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: What is he that you ask for, niece?

lines.speaker: Hero
lines.text: My cousin means Signior Benedick of Padua.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: O! he is returned, and as pleasant as ever he was.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: He set up his bills here in Messina and challenged Cupid at the flight;

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: and my uncle's fool, reading the challenge, subscribed for Cupid, and

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: challenged him at the bird-bolt. I pray you, how many hath he killed

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: and eaten in these wars?

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: But how many hath he killed? for, indeed, I promised to eat all of his

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: killing.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: Faith, niece, you tax Signior Benedick too much; but he'll be meet with

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: you, I doubt it not.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: He hath done good service, lady, in these wars.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: You had musty victual, and he hath holp to eat it; he is a very

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: valiant trencher-man; he hath an excellent stomach.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: And a good soldier too, lady.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: And a good soldier to a lady; but what is he to a lord?

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: A lord to a lord, a man to a man; stuffed with all honourable

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: virtues.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: It is so indeed; he is no less than a stuffed man; but for the

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: stuffing,--well, we are all mortal.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: You must not, sir, mistake my niece. There is a kind of merry war

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: betwixt Signior Benedick and her; they never meet but there's a

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: skirmish of wit between them.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: Alas! he gets nothing by that. In our last conflict four of his five

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: wits went halting off, and now is the whole man governed with one! so

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: that if he have wit enough to keep himself warm, let him bear it for a

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: difference between himself and his horse; for it is all the wealth that

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: he hath left to be known a reasonable creature. Who is his companion

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: now? He hath every month a new sworn brother.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: Is't possible?

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: Very easily possible: he wears his faith but as the fashion of his

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: hat; it ever changes with the next block.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: I see, lady, the gentleman is not in your books.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: No;an he were, I would burn my study. But, I pray you, who is his

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: companion? Is there no young squarer now that will make a voyage with

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: him to the devil?

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: He is most in the company of the right noble Claudio.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: O Lord, he will hang upon him like a disease: he is sooner caught than

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: the pestilence, and the taker runs presently mad. God help the noble

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: Claudio! If he have caught the Benedick, it will cost him a thousand

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: pound ere a' be cured.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: I will hold friends with you, lady.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: Do, good friend.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: You will never run mad, niece.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: No, not till a hot January.

lines.speaker: Messenger
lines.text: Don Pedro is approached.

stage_directions: Enter DON PEDRO, DON JOHN, CLAUDIO, BENEDICK, BALTHAZAR, and Others.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: Good Signior Leonato, you are come to meet your trouble: the fashion

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: of the world is to avoid cost, and you encounter it.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: Never came trouble to my house in the likeness of your Grace, for

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: trouble being gone, comfort should remain; but when you depart from me,

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: sorrow abides and happiness takes his leave.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: You embrace your charge too willingly. I think this is your daughter.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: Her mother hath many times told me so.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Were you in doubt, sir, that you asked her?

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: Signior Benedick, no; for then were you a child.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: You have it full, Benedick: we may guess by this what you are, being

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: a man. Truly the lady fathers herself. Be happy, lady, for you are

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: like an honourable father.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: If Signior Leonato be her father, she would not have his head on her

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: shoulders for all Messina, as like him as she is.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: I wonder that you will still be talking, Signior Benedick: nobody

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: marks you.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: What! my dear Lady Disdain, are you yet living?

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: Is it possible Disdain should die while she hath such meet food to

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: feed it as Signior Benedick? Courtesy itself must convert to disdain

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: if you come in her presence.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Then is courtesy a turncoat. But it is certain I am loved of all ladies,

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: only you excepted; and I would I could find in my heart that I had not

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: a hard heart;for, truly, I love none.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: A dear happiness to women: they would else have been troubled with a

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: pernicious suitor. I thank God and my cold blood, I am of your humour

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: for that. I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: loves me.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: God keep your ladyship still in that mind;so some gentleman or other

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: shallscape a predestinate scratched face.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: Scratching could not make it worse, an 'twere such a face as yours

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: were.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Well, you are a rare parrot-teacher.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: A bird of my tongue is better than a beast of yours.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: I would my horse had the speed of your tongue, and so good a

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: continuer. But keep your way, i' God's name; I have done.

lines.speaker: Beatrice
lines.text: You always end with a jade's trick: I know you of old.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: That is the sum of all, Leonato: Signior Claudio, and Signior Benedick,

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: my dear friend Leonato hath invited you all. I tell him we shall stay

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: here at the least a month, and he heartly prays some occasion may

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: detain us longer: I dare swear he is no hypocrite, but prays from his

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: heart.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: If you swear, my lord, you shall not be forsworn.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: Let me bid you welcome, my lord: being reconciled to the prince your

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: brother, I owe you all duty.

lines.speaker: Don John
lines.text: I thank you: I am not of many words, but I thank you.

lines.speaker: Leonato
lines.text: Please it your Grace lead on?

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: Your hand, Leonato;we will go together.

stage_directions: Exeunt all but BENEDICK and CLAUDIO.

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: Benedick, didst thou note the daughter of Signior Leonato?

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: I noted her not; but I looked on her.

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: Is she not a modest young lady?

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Do you question me, as an honest man should do, for my simple true

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: judgment; or would you have me speak after my custom, as being a

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: professed tyrant to their sex?

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: No; I pray thee speak in sober judgment.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Why, i' faith, methinks she's too low for a high praise, too brown

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: for a fair praise, and too little for a great praise; only this

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: commendation I can afford her, that were she other than she is, she

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: were unhandsome, and being no other but as she is, I do not like her.

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: Thou thinkest I am in sport: I pray thee tell me truly how thou

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: likest her.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Would you buy her, that you enquire after her?

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: Can the world buy such a jewel?

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Yea, and a case to put it into. But speak you this with a sad brow, or

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: do you play the flouting Jack, to tell us Cupid is a good hare-finder,

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: and Vulcan a rare carpenter? Come, in what key shall a man take you,

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: to go in the song?

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: In mine eye she is the sweetest lady that ever I looked on.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: I can see yet without spectacles and I see no such matter:  there's

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: her cousin an she were not possessed with a fury, exceeds her as much

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: in beauty as the first of May doth the last of December. But I hope you

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: have no intent to turn husband, have you?

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: I would scarce trust myself, though I had sworn to the contrary, if Hero

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: would be my wife.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Is't come to this, i' faith? Hath not the world one man but he will wear

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: his cap with suspicion? Shall I never see a bachelor of threescore

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: again? Go to, i' faith; an thou wilt needs thrust thy neck into a yoke,

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: wear the print of it and sigh away Sundays. Look! Don Pedro is returned

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: to seek you.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: What secret hath held you here, that you followed not to Leonato's?

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: I would your Grace would constrain me to tell.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: I charge thee on thy allegiance.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: You hear, Count Claudio: I can be secret as a dumb man; I would have

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: you think so; but on my allegiance mark you this, on my allegiance: he

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: is in love. With who? now that is your Grace's part. Mark how short his

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: answer is:  with Hero, Leonato's short daughter.

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: If this were so, so were it uttered.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: Like the old tale, my lord: 'it is not so, nor 'twas not so; but indeed,

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: God forbid it should be so.'

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: If my passion change not shortly. God forbid it should be otherwise.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: Amen, if you love her; for the lady is very well worthy.

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: You speak this to fetch me in, my lord.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: By my troth, I speak my thought.

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: And in faith, my lord, I spoke mine.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: And by my two faiths and troths, my lord, I spoke mine.

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: That I love her, I feel.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: That she is worthy, I know.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: That I neither feel how she should be loved nor know how she should

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: be worthy, is the opinion that fire cannot melt out of me: I will die

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: in it at the stake.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: Thou wast ever an obstinate heretic in the despite of beauty.

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: And never could maintain his part but in the force of his will.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: That a woman conceived me, I thank her; that she brought me up, I

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: likewise give her most humble thanks; but that I will have a recheat

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: winded in my forehead, or hang my bugle in an invisible baldrick, all

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: women shall pardon me. Because I will not do them the wrong to mistrust

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: any, I will do myself the right to trust none; and the fine is,--for

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: the which I may go the finer,--I will live a bachelor.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: I shall see thee, ere I die, look pale with love.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: With anger, with sickness, or with hunger, my lord; not with love: prove

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: that ever I lose more blood with love than I will get again with

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: drinking, pick out mine eyes with a ballad-maker's pen and hang me up at

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: the door of a brothel-house for the sign of blind Cupid.

lines.text: Well, if ever thou dost fall from this faith, thou wilt prove a notable

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: argument.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: If I do, hang me in a bottle like a cat and shoot at me; and he that

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: hits me, let him be clapped on the shoulder and called Adam.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: Well, as time shall try: 'In time the savage bull doth bear the yoke.'

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: The savage bull may; but if ever the sensible Benedick bear it, pluck

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: off the bull's horns and set them in my forehead; and let me be vilely

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: painted, and in such great letters as they write, 'Here is good horse

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: to hire,' let them signify under my sign 'Here you may see Benedick

lines.speaker: Benedick

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: If this should ever happen, thou wouldst be horn-mad.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: Nay, if Cupid have not spent all his quiver in Venice, thou wilt quake

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: for this shortly.

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: I look for an earthquake too then.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: Well, you will temporize with the hours. In the meantime, good Signior

lines.speaker: Don Pedro

lines.text: I have almost matter enough in me for such an embassage; and so I

lines.text: commit you--

lines.speaker: Benedick

lines.speaker: Benedick
lines.text: you flout old ends any further, examine your conscience: and so I leave

lines.speaker: Benedick

lines.text: O! my lord,

lines.text: When you went onward on this ended action,

lines.text: I looked upon her with a soldier's eye,

lines.text: That lik'd, but had a rougher task in hand

lines.text: Have left their places vacant, in their rooms

lines.text: Come thronging soft and delicate desires,

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: All prompting me how fair young Hero is,

lines.text: Thou wilt be like a lover presently,

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: And tire the hearer with a book of words.

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: If thou dost love fair Hero, cherish it,

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: And I will break with her, and with her father,

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: And thou shalt have her. Was't not to this end

lines.speaker: Don Pedro
lines.text: That thou began'st to twist so fine a story?

lines.text: How sweetly you do minister to love,

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: That know love's grief by his complexion!

lines.speaker: Claudio
lines.text: But lest my liking might too sudden seem,

lines.text: How now, brother! Where is my cousin your son? Hath he provided

lines.text: He is very busy about it. But, brother, I can tell you strange
